senses.gloss: Accepting what happens without acting or resisting.
examples: He stayed *passive* while the others argued about the bill.
Her *passive* attitude toward the problem frustrated everyone.
Kids get more *passive* the longer they sit in front of a screen.

senses.gloss: In grammar, of a verb form in which the subject receives the action.
examples: The sentence *The window was broken* uses the *passive* voice.
Teachers often tell students to avoid the *passive* voice.
In a *passive* construction the doer may not be mentioned at all.

senses.gloss: Working with no active effort, power or equipment.
examples: *Passive* income lets him work three days a week.
*Passive* smoking is dangerous for small children.

position: both — nearly always before a noun; *Those days are past* is formal
contrast: *Past* is also a preposition (*drive past the school*) and a noun (*in the past*); only the use with a noun is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Gone by; belonging to the time before now.
examples: I've been sick for the *past* few days.
Over the *past* year the company has doubled in size.
*Past* experience tells me not to trust that website.

senses.gloss: Former — holding a position earlier but not now.
examples: She is a *past* president of the association.
The award goes to a *past* winner every tenth year.

contrast: *Pastel* is also a noun — a soft chalk for drawing, and the drawing made with it.

senses.gloss: Soft and pale in color.
examples: The nursery is painted in *pastel* colors.
She wore a *pastel* blue dress to the wedding.
The walls are *pastel*, which makes the room feel bigger.

senses.gloss: Heated to kill harmful bacteria, so that it keeps longer.
examples: Only *pasteurized* milk is sold in American supermarkets.
The cheese is made from milk that has not been *pasteurized*.
Check the label to see whether the juice is *pasteurized*.

senses.gloss: Showing country life as pleasant and peaceful.
examples: The painting shows a *pastoral* scene with sheep and a stream.
He writes *pastoral* poetry about the farm where he grew up.

senses.gloss: Relating to a priest's or minister's care for people.
examples: The church offers *pastoral* counseling to families.
*Pastoral* duties take up most of her week.

contrast: The British noun *pasty* (a meat pie) rhymes with *nasty*; the adjective rhymes with *tasty*.

senses.gloss: Pale and unhealthy-looking.
examples: He looked *pasty* after a week indoors.
By February everyone's face is *pastier* than it was in July.
She has a *pasty* complexion that burns in ten minutes.

senses.gloss: Thick and sticky, like paste.
examples: The sauce turned *pasty* as it cooled.
Add water until the powder is no longer *pasty*.

contrast: Don't confuse the adjective with the verb *pat* (*pat the dog*) or the idiom *have it down pat*, meaning 'know it perfectly'.

senses.gloss: Too quick and easy to be convincing; sounding prepared in advance.
examples: He gave a *pat* answer that satisfied nobody.
The movie ends with a *pat* solution to a serious problem.
Her explanation sounded a little too *pat*.

senses.gloss: Appearing in separate small areas rather than evenly.
examples: *Patchy* fog is expected along the coast tonight.
The grass is *patchy* where the dog sleeps.

senses.gloss: Good in some parts and bad in others.
examples: His knowledge of the subject is *patchy*.
Cell service gets *patchier* the farther you drive.

contrast: *Patent* is far more common as a noun and a verb (*file a patent*, *patent an invention*).

senses.gloss: Completely obvious; impossible to deny.
examples: That is *patent* nonsense and everyone in the room knew it.
The article contained a *patent* lie about the mayor.

senses.gloss: Of leather: treated to have a hard, shiny surface.
examples: She wore black *patent* shoes with the dress.
The purse is made of red *patent* leather.

senses.gloss: Protected by a patent, so that only the owner may make or sell it.
examples: The company uses a *patented* process to purify the water.
Their *patented* design keeps the cup from tipping over.

senses.gloss: Informal: unmistakably a particular person's own.
examples: He greeted us with his *patented* grin.
She answered with her *patented* mix of charm and steel.

senses.gloss: Like a father; showing a father's care.
examples: He felt a surge of *paternal* pride at the graduation.
The coach takes a *paternal* interest in his players.

senses.gloss: Related through the father.
examples: My *paternal* grandmother came from Poland.
The condition is passed down through the *paternal* line.

senses.gloss: Making decisions for other people as if they could not decide for themselves.
examples: The policy is well meant but deeply *paternalistic*.
Patients resent a *paternalistic* doctor who won't explain anything.
Older companies tend to be more *paternalistic* toward their workers.

senses.gloss: Unable to stop doing something, in a way that seems like an illness.
examples: He is a *pathological* liar — he can't help it.
She has a *pathological* fear of being late.

senses.gloss: Relating to disease and its causes.
examples: The lab found no *pathological* changes in the tissue.
*Pathological* tests confirmed the diagnosis.

senses.gloss: Controlled by men, or organized so that men hold the power.
examples: She grew up in a strongly *patriarchal* household.
The novel is a quiet attack on a *patriarchal* society.
Village life there is still more *patriarchal* than in the capital.

contrast: *Patrician* is also a noun — a member of the old Roman nobility.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or typical of the upper class.
examples: He speaks with a *patrician* accent.
Her *patrician* manners set her apart at the meeting.
The family lived in a *patrician* house above the river.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing strong love for one's country.
examples: The Fourth of July is full of *patriotic* songs and parades.
He isn't *patriotic* about much, but he loves the anthem.
Nothing makes her feel more *patriotic* than the Olympics.

contrast: The verb *patronize* has a second, neutral meaning — to be a regular customer of a store.

senses.gloss: Treating someone as if they were less intelligent or important than you.
examples: Don't use that *patronizing* tone with me.
The article is *patronizing* toward first-time voters.
Explaining it a third time would be *patronizing*.

ru: узорчатый, с рисунком; созданный по образцу

senses.gloss: Decorated with a repeated design.
examples: She chose a *patterned* wallpaper for the hallway.
The chairs are *patterned*, so the rug should be plain.

senses.gloss: Made to follow the model of something else.
examples: The new law is *patterned* after the one in California.
Their school is *patterned* on a British boarding school.

senses.gloss: Covered with a hard surface such as asphalt, concrete or stone.
examples: Turn left where the road becomes *paved*.
A *paved* path leads down to the lake.
Their driveway is *paved* with red brick.

senses.gloss: Happening automatically, as a trained reaction to a signal.
examples: My dog has a *Pavlovian* response to the sound of the can opener.
Checking the phone the second it buzzes is a *Pavlovian* reflex.
The ad works on a simple *Pavlovian* association.

position: after the noun — also after a verb: *The fee is payable in advance*

senses.gloss: That must be paid, or may be paid, at a stated time or to a stated person.
examples: The deposit is *payable* when you sign the lease.
Make the check *payable* to the county clerk.

senses.gloss: Bringing in money; profitable.

senses.gloss: Who pays for what they get.
examples: *Paying* customers get free shipping.
The inn takes *paying* guests all summer.

senses.gloss: Wanting to avoid fighting and to live quietly.
examples: They are a *peace-loving* people who have not fought a war in centuries.
My grandfather was a quiet, *peace-loving* man.
The group calls itself *peace-loving*, but its actions say otherwise.

senses.gloss: Quiet and calm; free from noise or worry.
examples: The cabin is the most *peaceful* place I know.
She looked *peaceful* in her sleep.
Evenings here are more *peaceful* than in the city.

senses.gloss: Without war or violence.
examples: They reached a *peaceful* settlement after months of talks.
The march stayed *peaceful* all afternoon.

senses.gloss: Concerned with keeping peace between groups that have been fighting.
examples: The country sent a *peacekeeping* force to the border.
*Peacekeeping* troops patrol the area in white vehicles.

senses.gloss: Informal: fine, excellent — often said sarcastically.

senses.gloss: Colored or flavored like a peach.

This white wine is *peachier* than the last bottle.

contrast: The British idiom *go pear-shaped*, meaning 'go badly wrong', is not used in American English.

senses.gloss: Narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, like a pear.
examples: The vase is *pear-shaped* and very heavy.
She has a *pear-shaped* figure and shops accordingly.
A *pear-shaped* diamond sat in the middle of the ring.

senses.gloss: Shining softly and whitish, like a pearl.
examples: He flashed a smile full of *pearly* white teeth.
The inside of the shell is smooth and *pearly*.
A *pearly* light came through the morning fog.

takes: *to* + noun, in the 'belonging only to' sense

senses.gloss: Strange or odd.
examples: There was a *peculiar* smell in the basement.
He has a *peculiar* way of holding his fork.
The story gets more *peculiar* the longer you listen.

senses.gloss: Belonging only to one person, place or group.
examples: That accent is *peculiar* to the islands.

senses.gloss: Relating to teaching and to how it is done.
examples: The school changed textbooks for *pedagogical* reasons.

There is no *pedagogical* value in copying the list twice.

senses.gloss: Caring too much about small rules and details.
examples: I don't want to be *pedantic*, but the date is wrong.
His *pedantic* corrections slowed the whole meeting down.
Nobody is more *pedantic* about commas than an editor.

contrast: *Pedestrian* is also a very common noun — a person on foot.

senses.gloss: Dull and ordinary; showing no imagination.
examples: The food was good but the wine list was *pedestrian*.
Critics called the second album *pedestrian*.
His prose is more *pedestrian* than his ideas.

senses.gloss: Relating to people who are walking.
examples: A new *pedestrian* bridge crosses the highway.
*Pedestrian* traffic downtown has doubled since the street closed.

contrast: American spelling is *pediatric*; British writes *paediatric*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the medical care of children.
examples: She works in the *pediatric* ward at the county hospital.
We took him to a *pediatric* dentist.
The drug has not been approved for *pediatric* use.

contrast: *Keep your eyes peeled* means 'watch carefully' — nothing is actually peeled.

senses.gloss: With the skin or outer layer taken off.
examples: The recipe calls for two *peeled* potatoes.
Buy the shrimp already *peeled* and dinner takes half the time.
He handed me a *peeled* orange.

comparison: not gradable — an absolute: something *peerless* has no equal, so *more peerless* says nothing

senses.gloss: Better than anyone or anything else of its kind.
examples: She was a *peerless* storyteller.
The museum holds a *peerless* collection of early maps.

senses.gloss: Mildly annoyed.

He looked *peeved* about having to wait.
I'm a little *peeved* at my brother right now.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed and quick to complain.
examples: He gets *peevish* when he hasn't eaten.
She answered in a *peevish* voice.
The baby is *peevish* by late afternoon.

senses.gloss: Expressing disapproval or contempt.
examples: The word 'bureaucrat' is usually *pejorative*.
He used the term in a *pejorative* sense.
She avoids *pejorative* labels when she writes about patients.

senses.gloss: Relating to the bowl-shaped set of bones at the base of the spine.
examples: The X-ray showed a *pelvic* fracture.
*Pelvic* floor exercises help after childbirth.
He felt *pelvic* pain for weeks after the fall.

senses.gloss: Relating to the punishment of crimes.
examples: The state overhauled its *penal* code last year.
Conditions in the *penal* colony were brutal.
*Penal* reform has support in both parties.

position: both — also right after a noun: *patent pending*
contrast: *Pending* is also a preposition meaning 'until': *pending further review*.

senses.gloss: Waiting to be decided or settled.
examples: Her application is still *pending*.
There are three *pending* lawsuits against the company.
The sale is *pending* until the inspection is done.

senses.gloss: About to happen.
examples: Everyone in the office knew about his *pending* retirement.
The *pending* storm closed the schools a day early.

senses.gloss: Sharp and strong enough to go through or into something.
examples: He fixed me with a *penetrating* stare.
The cheese has a *penetrating* smell you notice from the hall.
Her voice is *penetrating* enough to carry across the gym.

senses.gloss: Showing deep understanding.
examples: She asked a *penetrating* question about the budget.
The book offers a *penetrating* analysis of the crisis.

senses.gloss: Sorry for having done something wrong.
examples: He came back *penitent* and asked to be forgiven.
She wrote a *penitent* letter to her former boss.
The boy looked *penitent*, but he did it again a week later.

senses.gloss: Having no money at all.
examples: He arrived in the city *penniless* and slept in a park.
The war left thousands of families *penniless*.
She married a *penniless* musician and never regretted it.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to spend even small amounts of money.
examples: His *penny-pinching* habits drive his family crazy.
The *penny-pinching* landlord won't replace the heater.
After years of being *penny-pinching*, they finally took a real vacation.

senses.gloss: Thinking deeply about something, often in a quiet and slightly sad way.
examples: She grew *pensive* when we mentioned her old school.
He sat by the window with a *pensive* look.
The music is *pensive* rather than sad.

position: attributive only — before a noun; after a verb it is written without the hyphen: *The anger had been pent up for years*
form: compound — an old past participle of *pen*, 'to shut in', + *up*

senses.gloss: Held inside for a long time and not let out.
examples: All his *pent-up* frustration came out at once.
There is a lot of *pent-up* demand for new housing.
The dog has *pent-up* energy after a day indoors.

contrast: Always capitalized; *Pentecostal* is also a noun for a member of the church.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a Christian movement that stresses direct experience of the Holy Spirit.
examples: They attend a *Pentecostal* church on the south side of town.
*Pentecostal* services often include singing and clapping.
The *Pentecostal* movement grew quickly in Latin America.

contrast: *Penultimate* does not mean 'the very last' or 'the ultimate' — it means second to last.

senses.gloss: Second to last — the one right before the final one.
examples: Stress falls on the *penultimate* syllable in most Polish words.

She was eliminated in the *penultimate* round.

senses.gloss: Tasting strongly of pepper, or hot in the mouth.
examples: The soup is a little too *peppery* for the kids.
Arugula has a *peppery* bite.

senses.gloss: Quick-tempered and sharp.
examples: The old judge had a *peppery* manner.
He wrote a *peppery* letter to the editor.

senses.gloss: Lively and full of energy.
examples: The playlist is *peppy* enough to run to.

position: both — before a noun (*per capita income*) and after one (*income per capita*)

senses.gloss: Counted for each person in a population.

senses.gloss: Quick to notice and understand things.

senses.gloss: Relating to how the senses take in and interpret information.

senses.gloss: Giving an order in a way that allows no refusal or discussion.

contrast: *Perennial* is also a noun for such a plant: *We planted perennials along the fence*.

senses.gloss: Happening again and again, year after year.

senses.gloss: Of a plant: living for more than two years.

senses.gloss: Having small holes made in it, often a line of them so it can be torn.

senses.gloss: Given a pleasant smell, or filled with one.

senses.gloss: Very dangerous.

senses.gloss: Relating to the gums and the tissue that holds the teeth.

senses.gloss: Cheerful, lively and confident.

senses.gloss: Lasting for a very long time or forever; not meant to change.

contrast: *Perverse* means stubbornly contrary; *perverted* is the word for sexually abnormal.

senses.gloss: Deliberately doing the opposite of what is wanted or sensible.
examples: He takes a *perverse* pleasure in proving people wrong.
It would be *perverse* to refuse their help now.

senses.gloss: Going against what is right or natural.
examples: The rule has the *perverse* effect of punishing the people it was meant to help.
There is something *perverse* about a system that rewards failure.

senses.gloss: Sexually abnormal in a way that most people find disgusting.
examples: The messages were *perverted* and frightening.
He was fired over a *perverted* joke at the company party.

senses.gloss: Twisted away from what is right or true.
examples: They act out of a *perverted* sense of loyalty.
The original idea has been completely *perverted*.

senses.gloss: Informal: annoying, in a small and constant way.
examples: Those *pesky* mosquitoes ruined the evening.
I finally fixed that *pesky* leak under the sink.
The *peskier* the question, the longer he takes to answer it.

senses.gloss: Expecting that bad things will happen.
examples: He is *pessimistic* about his chances of getting the job.
The report takes a *pessimistic* view of next year.
She has grown more *pessimistic* since the layoffs.

contrast: *Pet* is much more often a noun (*feed the pet*) or a verb (*pet the dog*).

senses.gloss: Favorite; that one person cares about more than other things.
examples: Recycling is her *pet* project at the office.
People who chew gum loudly are his *pet* peeve.

senses.gloss: Kept or treated as a pet animal.
examples: They have a *pet* rabbit named Waffle.
The boy carried a *pet* snake into class.

contrast: *Petite* is said of women and of women's clothing sizes; a small man is *short* or *slight*.

senses.gloss: Small and slim — said of a woman or of women's clothing sizes.
examples: She is *petite* and has trouble finding pants that fit.
The store has a *petite* section near the back.
Her sister is even more *petite* than she is.

senses.gloss: Small and unimportant.
examples: He was arrested for *petty* theft.
The office keeps forty dollars in *petty* cash.

senses.gloss: Caring too much about small things, in a mean way.
examples: Don't be *petty* about who paid for lunch.
The argument got *pettier* by the minute.

senses.gloss: Bad-tempered in a childish way, over something small.
examples: He gave a *petulant* shrug and turned away.
Her voice turned *petulant* when the waiter said they were out of it.
The candidate sounded *petulant* rather than presidential.

senses.gloss: Shaped like, or relating to, the male sex organ.
examples: The monument has an unmistakably *phallic* shape.
Critics read the tower as a *phallic* symbol.
The sculpture is deliberately *phallic*.

contrast: *Phantom* is more often a noun — a ghost.

senses.gloss: Not really there, although it seems or feels real.
examples: He still feels *phantom* pain in the leg he lost.
The audit turned up dozens of *phantom* employees on the payroll.
She heard a *phantom* ringing and checked her pocket.
